buying-stock|restaurants-and-hospitality.h1: Finance for buying stock in restaurants and hospitality
buying-stock|restaurants-and-hospitality.title: Stock Finance for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
buying-stock|restaurants-and-hospitality.desc: How restaurants, cafés, bars and hotels finance food, drink and consumables ahead of busy periods, and which finance types suit. Get matched with a broker.
buying-stock|restaurants-and-hospitality.lead: Food and drink go off, supplier bills fall due quickly and card takings arrive daily, so the finance needs to move at the same pace.
intro: Hospitality stock behaves differently from stock in most other trades. Fresh produce may last days, wine and spirits can sit in a cellar for months, and suppliers often want payment within seven to thirty days. A venue heading into December, a summer terrace season or a large event booking may need to buy far more than usual before any of the extra takings arrive. Lenders will also ask how reliable that trade is.

Because most venues take payment by card the same day, lenders can see the daily revenue that would repay a facility. That is why a merchant cash advance, a revolving credit facility or a short unsecured loan are the usual starting points. Which suits depends on how fast the stock turns and whether the extra purchase is a one-off or something that recurs every few weeks. Quiet weeks matter as much as busy ones.
uses: Christmas and event season
Build up wine, spirits, dry goods and frozen lines before December party bookings, then repay as the covers come through.
Stocking a cellar or bar
Buy a case-quantity order of wines or spirits at a supplier’s better price, where the saving can offset the cost of finance.
Opening a second site
Pay for the first fill of kitchen stock, glassware, linen and consumables before the new site has taken its first booking.
Seasonal tourist trade
Cover heavier weekly buying across a coastal or festival season, when suppliers expect payment before the peak takings are in.
fit: Repayment follows card takings

A merchant cash advance is repaid as a share of daily card sales, so repayments rise in busy weeks and ease in quiet ones. For example, a restaurant needing £25,000 of stock before December might find this suits better than fixed monthly payments through a slow January.
Revolving facilities for steady buying

Venues that buy every week can use a revolving credit facility, drawing for a large order and repaying as takings arrive. Lenders look at monthly card turnover, how consistent it is across seasons, and how much is already owed to suppliers.
A loan for one planned purchase

A short unsecured loan suits a single known order, such as a pre-bought wine allocation. Terms are usually matched to how quickly the stock will sell, and lenders will check recent bank statements, accounts and director details.
considerations: Perishable stock is poor security
Fresh food cannot be pledged or held for long, so finance for it should be repaid fast. Borrowing over a long term for produce that is eaten within a week means paying for money you no longer need.
Wastage and over-ordering
A forecast for a busy week can miss, and unsold fresh stock is a straight loss. Order in stages where suppliers allow it, and borrow for what you are confident of selling.
Quiet months still come

Fixed repayments in January or February can hurt a venue whose takings fall sharply. Ask a broker about structures that flex with sales, and check whether supplier terms alone could cover part of the order.
faqs: Can I get a loan to buy stock for my restaurant?

Often, yes. Lenders look at your card takings, accounts and how long you have traded. A merchant cash advance, revolving credit facility or short unsecured loan are common routes. A broker can compare options once they have seen your figures, though Loanleaf does not give advice or guarantee any outcome.
Is a merchant cash advance suitable for a pub or café?

It can be, because repayment is taken as a percentage of daily card sales and so moves with trade. It is usually costlier overall than a conventional loan, so compare the total repayable, not just the monthly feel of it. A broker can explain the costs for your case.
How long should finance for food stock last?

Usually as short as the stock cycle allows. Fresh food turns in days or weeks, while wine and spirits may take months. A broker can suggest terms that match how quickly your particular lines sell, rather than a long loan for goods already eaten.
Will lenders look at seasonal swings in my sales?

Yes. They tend to review twelve months of bank statements or card data to see how takings move through the year. A venue with a strong summer and a quiet winter should explain that clearly, as it affects how repayments are set up.
What if a supplier offers a discount for bulk buying?

It can be worth taking, if the saving is clearly larger than the full cost of the finance and the stock will not spoil or sit unsold. Work through the arithmetic with your accountant, including any fees, before borrowing for it. Some venues also ask suppliers for staged deliveries.

hiring-staff|restaurants-and-hospitality.h1: Finance for hiring staff in restaurants and hospitality
hiring-staff|restaurants-and-hospitality.title: Hiring Staff Finance for Restaurants and Hotels | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|restaurants-and-hospitality.desc: How restaurants, bars, cafés and hotels finance chefs, front-of-house teams and seasonal staff, and which finance types tend to suit. Get matched with a broker.
hiring-staff|restaurants-and-hospitality.lead: Kitchens and dining rooms need a full team before the doors open, and wages start long before the covers do.
intro: A hospitality business often has to hire ahead of demand. A new head chef may need two or three weeks of paid prep, a second site needs a full front-of-house team before its first booking, and a summer season needs temporary staff trained and on the rota before the first busy weekend. Employer National Insurance, holiday pay and uniform costs add to the wage bill, and rises in the minimum wage can lift costs for the whole team at once.

Wages are the largest regular outgoing for most venues, so lenders look closely at how comfortably takings cover them. Unsecured loans, merchant cash advances repaid from card sales and revolving credit facilities are the usual options. The choice depends on whether the hire is permanent, seasonal or tied to a new opening. Lenders will also look at how much of takings already goes on payroll before deciding what extra they are comfortable with.
uses: Staffing a new opening
Pay a chef team, bar staff and managers during the weeks of training and soft launch before the new site is trading at full volume.
Seasonal summer or Christmas team
Take on and train extra waiting and kitchen staff for a peak, covering the wages until the busier takings arrive.
Hiring a head chef or manager
Bring in an experienced hire on a salary the venue cannot yet carry from its own margins, as part of a menu or format change.
Training and certification
Cover food hygiene, licensing, allergen and first-aid training for new starters so they can work a full shift safely.
fit: Matching the loan to the peak

For a seasonal team, a short unsecured loan or merchant cash advance can line up repayments with the busy months. For example, a hotel hiring eight extra staff for six months might borrow £30,000 and repay it over a similar period.
Revolving cover for uneven weeks

A revolving credit facility suits venues whose wages are steady while takings swing, because the business draws in a quiet week and repays after a busy one. Lenders check consistency of card revenue and how much headroom already exists.
What lenders review

Expect questions on payroll as a share of takings, how long the venue has traded and what the hire is expected to add. Recent accounts, bank statements and director details are usual, and an unsecured lender may ask for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Wages outlast the loan
The loan covers the early months, but the salary goes on. Check that takings will carry the new role once repayments end, and be cautious on a hire that only pays back at full capacity.
High turnover in the sector
Hospitality staff move on more often than in many industries, so training money can walk out of the door. Budget for replacing people, not just recruiting once.
Rising baseline costs
A minimum wage increase lifts every rate on the rota, not just the new hire’s. Build that into your numbers, and avoid borrowing to the limit for a hire that leaves no margin.
faqs: Can I borrow to pay wages while a new restaurant opens?

Many operators do, usually with an unsecured loan or a facility repaid from takings. Lenders will want to see the plan, the other costs and how the business will cover wages once open. A broker can explain what a lender is likely to ask for.
What finance suits temporary summer staff?

Short-term options often fit best, such as a merchant cash advance repaid from card sales or a short unsecured loan. Because the staff are only needed for the season, a long-term commitment could outlast the benefit. A broker can compare the choices.
Will lenders count my existing wage bill?

Yes. They look at payroll as a share of revenue, and whether profit after wages can cover repayments. Venues with tight margins may find lenders more cautious, so keep recent payroll figures and accounts ready. Private income is also considered, and so is how steady each source is. A broker can advise how your own mix is likely to be viewed.
Can I finance recruitment agency fees?

Some businesses include them in a general working-capital loan. Agency fees can be a meaningful lump sum, so it may be worth asking the agency about staged payment first. A broker can say whether a loan is likely to be sensible for the amount.
Do I need a personal guarantee?

Unsecured lenders commonly ask directors for one, particularly for smaller limited companies. It means you could be personally liable if the business cannot repay. Read the terms carefully, and take advice from your solicitor or accountant before signing. It is worth checking exactly what is being guaranteed.

buying-stock|construction-and-trades.h1: Finance for buying stock in construction and trades
buying-stock|construction-and-trades.title: Stock and Materials Finance for Construction | Loanleaf
buying-stock|construction-and-trades.desc: How builders, electricians, plumbers and contractors finance materials and trade stock before jobs are paid for, and which finance types suit. Get matched.
buying-stock|construction-and-trades.lead: Materials are bought up front and jobs are paid weeks or months later, so the gap between the two is where finance helps.
intro: A trade business pays its builders’ merchant or wholesaler long before the customer pays it. A kitchen fit-out, a block of rewires or a roofing contract can mean thousands of pounds of materials on site within days, while the main contractor pays on 30 to 60 day terms and may hold back retention. Merchant credit limits can run out just when a big job needs the most stock. Lenders understand that rhythm.

Materials prices can also move quickly, so some firms buy ahead for contracts already won. Because the money that repays the finance usually comes from specific invoices, invoice finance and revolving credit facilities are common, with short unsecured loans for a one-off bulk purchase. The right choice depends on how the business is paid and who its customers are. Customer mix, rather than the size of the job alone, shapes what is available.
uses: Materials for a signed contract
Buy cable, pipe, timber or steel for a contract already won, so the job starts on schedule instead of waiting on a merchant’s limit.
Buying ahead of price rises
Lock in a price on a large order when suppliers signal increases, where the saving is clearly larger than the finance cost.
Stocking vans and a trade counter
Hold a working stock of fittings, fixings and common spares so engineers fix problems on the first visit.
Two sites at once
Fund materials for a second large job running alongside the first, before either has reached a valuation or an interim payment.
fit: Invoice finance when you wait to be paid

If the stock is bought for work invoiced to main contractors or housebuilders, invoice finance can release cash against those invoices. Lenders check who the customers are, the size of the invoices and any contractual retentions or set-off clauses.
A revolving facility for varied jobs

Firms whose materials spend swings job by job can use a revolving credit facility, drawing for each order and repaying as payments land. For example, a heating contractor might hold a £60,000 limit and use £35,000 of it for one job.
An unsecured loan for a single order

A short unsecured loan suits a one-off bulk purchase for a specific contract. Lenders look at the contract value, your trading history and recent bank statements, and may ask directors for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Retentions and slow payments
Retention can sit unpaid for 12 months or longer after a job finishes. If your repayments depend on that money, build in a buffer so the finance is not squeezed by delayed receipts.
Price swings cut both ways
Buying ahead only helps if prices rise, and a contract can be delayed or lost. Avoid borrowing for stock a firm order does not already require.
Merchant credit may be cheaper
A merchant’s own trade account, with an agreed credit limit, can be the lowest-cost way to buy materials. Try that first, and use finance for the amount it cannot cover.
faqs: Can I borrow to buy materials before a job is paid?

Often, yes. Invoice finance, a revolving credit facility or a short unsecured loan are common routes. Lenders will want to see the contract, your customers and your trading history. A broker can explain which fits, without Loanleaf offering advice or promising an outcome.
How does retention affect borrowing?

Retention is money held back until a job is signed off, so it is not available to repay finance in the meantime. Lenders may ask how much is outstanding and for how long. Keep a clear schedule of retentions, because it helps a broker present your cash flow honestly.
Is invoice finance suitable for a small electrician?

It can be, if the business invoices other companies, such as contractors or housing associations, on credit terms. It is less useful for firms paid by householders at completion. A broker can say whether your invoices would be accepted. Lenders look at who your customers are and how reliably they pay.
Should I use my builders’ merchant account instead?

If the limit is enough and the terms are fair, merchant credit is often cheap and simple. Finance becomes useful when a single contract needs more than the limit allows. Many firms combine the two. Many firms combine the two, using merchant credit for routine orders.
What if my contract is delayed after I buy materials?

You would still have to make repayments, so it is worth keeping a margin. Staging purchases and checking the programme before ordering can help. A broker can discuss structures with more flexible repayment timing. Many firms also agree a short extension with the supplier in advance.

hiring-staff|construction-and-trades.h1: Finance for hiring staff in construction and trades
hiring-staff|construction-and-trades.title: Hiring Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|construction-and-trades.desc: How builders, electricians, plumbers and contractors finance skilled hires, apprentices and extra crews while payments are slow, and which finance suits.
hiring-staff|construction-and-trades.lead: Skilled people are scarce in the trades, and new crews are paid weekly while the work is paid for in arrears.
intro: Trades businesses often win work they cannot yet staff. A contract needs two more electricians, a growing groundworks firm needs a second gang, or an owner who has been doing everything wants a site manager. Wages and employer costs begin on the first Friday, but payment for the job may follow valuations, certification and a 30 to 60 day invoice term, with retention held back on top. Lenders will want to see how firm the work behind it is.

That timing makes the sector a natural fit for finance linked to invoices, alongside unsecured loans for planned hires. Some firms are also converting self-employed subcontractors to employees, which changes costs as well as responsibilities. Lenders will be interested in the order book behind the hire, as well as the previous accounts. Tender pipelines, framework agreements and repeat clients all carry weight when a lender looks at a hire. A broker can explain how to present each.
uses: Crewing a contract you have won
Take on the operatives needed for a new contract and carry weekly wages until the first valuation is paid.
Apprentices and trainees
Cover supervision, college days, tools and PPE for apprentices, an investment that pays back over a few years.
A site manager or estimator
Add a senior hire so the owner can step away from the tools and price more work, supported by a salary the firm cannot yet fully carry.
Moving subcontractors to payroll
Bring regular subcontractors onto the payroll for greater control, absorbing employer National Insurance, pension and holiday pay.
fit: Invoice finance to bridge the pay gap

Where work is invoiced to contractors, developers or councils, invoice finance can release part of each invoice earlier. For example, a roofing firm hiring four roofers might draw against £80,000 of approved invoices. Lenders check customer quality and any retention or set-off terms.
Unsecured loans for planned growth

An unsecured loan gives a fixed sum with predictable repayments, which helps when a hire has a clear start date. Terms are usually chosen to give the new person time to become productive, and lenders may ask for a director’s personal guarantee.
A revolving facility for weekly payroll
A revolving credit facility lets you draw to cover a Friday wage run and repay when a valuation lands. Lenders review bank statements to see how payments and payroll line up through the month.
considerations: Work can dry up
Wages are fixed, while contracts end. Be sure the order book will keep the new crew busy for the full loan term, not just the first project.
Employment versus self-employment
Changing a subcontractor’s status has tax and legal implications. Speak to your accountant before relying on the cost estimates, and confirm they are right for your business.
Retention can delay repayments
Money held in retention is not available to meet wages or repayments. Keep a schedule of when it falls due, and borrow with room to spare.
faqs: Can I get a loan to pay wages on a new contract?

Yes, many trade firms use an unsecured loan, invoice finance or a revolving facility to carry wages until a first payment. Lenders will want to see the contract, your trading record and how the business covers costs. Outcomes depend on the individual case.
Does invoice finance work for subcontractors?

It can, where the invoices are to an established main contractor or developer. Lenders check the customer’s payment record and any contractual deductions. A broker can tell you whether your invoices would be considered. Signed contracts, framework agreements and a record of repeat clients all help a lender see why you are hiring.
How long should a loan for hiring last?

Long enough for the new person to cover their own cost, which in the trades may be a few months for an experienced operative or longer for an apprentice. A broker can help you match term to that timeline. Lenders also look at your bank statements to see how wages and payments line up.
Will lenders ask about my order book?

Usually, yes. They want to see that work exists to keep new staff busy. Signed contracts, tender pipelines and previous accounts all help, and a broker can advise on how to present them clearly. Agree the pay, hours and notice terms for new hires before you rely on the figures.
Is it safer to use agency labour first?

Agency staff cost more per hour but avoid long-term commitments, so some firms test demand that way. Compare the total cost over the likely period of work before choosing, and speak to your accountant. Check what any notice periods or minimum hours would mean for your costs.

buying-stock|retail.h1: Finance for buying stock in retail
buying-stock|retail.title: Stock Finance for Retailers | Loanleaf
buying-stock|retail.desc: How shops and retail groups finance seasonal buying, new ranges and bulk orders when stock is paid for months before it sells, and which finance suits.
buying-stock|retail.lead: A retailer pays for the winter range in the summer, so the money has to be found well before the tills ring.
intro: Retail buying runs on a calendar. Autumn and winter ranges are often ordered months ahead, Christmas stock can be committed to by late summer, and some suppliers ask for a deposit on order and the balance before shipment. The business pays out first, then waits for the footfall. A shop that buys cautiously risks empty shelves, while one that buys boldly ties up cash that rent, rates and wages also need.

Because most retailers take card payments daily, lenders can see the revenue that would repay a facility. Revolving credit facilities and merchant cash advances are common, with unsecured loans for a planned purchase. Where a retailer has a lot of unsold stock and no other assets, some lenders will also consider stock as part of the picture. Seasonal ranges are often the hardest to size. The calendar is the starting point.
uses: Christmas and Q4 buying
Pay deposits and balances on winter ranges months before the festive trading starts, then repay from takings.
Opening a second shop
Fill a new unit with stock and fixtures before it has made a single sale, without draining the first shop’s working cash.
A new category or brand
Take on a new product line, accepting a minimum order from the supplier before you know how it will sell.
Clearing a supplier’s end-of-line deal
Buy a large lot at a discount, where the margin remains attractive after the finance cost and the time to sell it.
fit: Revolving cover for the buying cycle

A revolving credit facility suits retailers who buy repeatedly through the year, since they can draw for each order and repay from takings. For example, a gift shop might hold a £50,000 limit and use most of it for September orders. Lenders check monthly revenue, margins and the facility’s history of use.
Merchant cash advance for card-heavy shops

Where most sales are on card, a merchant cash advance is repaid as a share of daily takings, so payments ease in a slow week. It is usually costlier than a conventional facility, so compare the total repayable.
One-off loans for a planned buy

An unsecured loan suits a single known purchase, such as a bulk order for a new range. Lenders look at accounts, bank statements and stock turnover, and directors may be asked for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Unsold stock is the real risk
Finance is only repaid easily if the goods sell. A fashion or seasonal range that misses can end in discounting, so test buying quantities carefully.
Match the term to sell-through
A long loan for stock that sells in ten weeks means interest long after the goods have gone. Flexible facilities, repaid as you sell, usually fit better.
Sale or return and supplier terms
Some suppliers will offer sale-or-return or 60-day terms. Ask before borrowing, since that can cut the amount you need to finance.
faqs: Can a small retailer borrow to buy stock?

Yes, if the company has traded for at least six months and has the turnover lenders look for. Revolving facilities, merchant cash advances and unsecured loans are common routes. A broker can compare these once they have seen your figures. Many firms also look at how long it would take to clear any unsold lines.
Is it better to use a facility or a loan for seasonal stock?

A revolving facility often fits better, because you draw for each order and repay as stock sells. A loan suits a single known purchase. The choice depends on how often you buy and how predictable your sales are. Loanleaf does not advise, but a broker can compare the two against your buying calendar.
Do lenders value the stock itself?

Some lenders can take it into account, but fast-moving or seasonal stock is hard to value and usually offers limited security. Most unsecured and card-based finance looks at your turnover and bank statements instead. Sell-through, margins and how long the stock has been in the shop all shape what a lender will accept.
What if I buy too much and have to discount?

You still have repayments to make, which is why it helps to borrow against realistic sales. Keep a buffer, review stock regularly and speak to a broker early if sales fall behind plan. Many retailers also negotiate extended payment terms with suppliers, which reduces the amount to borrow.
Can I finance imported stock?

Some specialist providers offer trade finance that pays overseas suppliers directly. Availability depends on the goods, the supplier and your trading history. A broker can say whether it is likely to be an option for you. Lenders often want to see supplier invoices alongside your sales history.

hiring-staff|retail.h1: Finance for hiring staff in retail
hiring-staff|retail.title: Hiring Finance for Retail Businesses | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|retail.desc: How shops and retail groups finance seasonal teams, new store staff and management hires, and which finance types tend to suit. Get matched with a broker.
hiring-staff|retail.lead: Stores need people on the floor before the customers arrive, and wages start long before the takings do.
intro: A retailer’s staffing needs rise and fall with the calendar. A shop might double its team for the run-up to Christmas, add weekend cover for the summer or take on a full complement of staff for a new unit before the opening day. Training, uniform, till systems and the first payroll all come first. The takings that justify the hire arrive afterwards, and sometimes only if the footfall is as good as forecast.

Retailers usually have daily card takings, which makes revolving credit facilities and merchant cash advances natural choices alongside unsecured loans. A temporary seasonal team calls for different finance from a permanent store manager or a head of e-commerce, and the terms should reflect that difference. It helps to be specific about how much extra trade each hire is expected to bring in, and how soon. Lenders will want to see last year’s monthly sales to judge the pattern, and a broker can explain what to include.
uses: Seasonal Christmas team
Recruit and train extra staff in October and November, ahead of the heaviest weeks of trading.
Staffing a new store
Cover a full opening team, from manager to weekend staff, while the new unit builds its customer base.
Extended opening hours
Add evening or Sunday staffing to test whether longer opening brings in enough sales to pay for itself.
Management and specialist hires
Employ a visual merchandiser, buyer or store manager whose salary the shop does not yet generate enough margin to carry.
fit: A revolving facility for payroll peaks

A facility can cover higher weekly wages through the peak and be repaid as takings arrive. For example, a clothing retailer might draw £15,000 in November for extra staff and clear it by January. Lenders check how consistent monthly revenue is across the year.
Card-based repayment

A merchant cash advance can suit a shop whose revenue is mostly card-based, because repayment is a share of daily sales. It is usually costlier than a conventional loan, so compare the total repayable first.
A loan for permanent hires

For a permanent store manager or a new unit’s team, an unsecured loan gives a fixed sum and predictable repayments. Lenders look at trading history, margins and wage costs as a share of sales, and may ask directors for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Wage costs are rising
Minimum wage increases lift payroll across the whole shop. Include that in the business plan, rather than assuming today’s hourly rates will hold.
Footfall is not guaranteed
A new store can take longer than expected to build trade. Borrow with a cushion, and consider hiring in stages as sales prove out.
Seasonal staff leave
Money spent on training seasonal workers does not carry forward into the next year. Keep training light and focused on what is needed for the season.
faqs: Can I get finance to hire seasonal staff?

Yes, short-term facilities and merchant cash advances are often used for this. Lenders will look at your sales through the previous year and your card takings. A broker can explain what is realistic for your own figures. Last year’s monthly figures are usually the first thing a lender asks for.
What suits a new store’s first wages?

A new unit has no trading history of its own, so lenders look at the whole company’s figures. An unsecured loan or revolving facility is common. A broker can say what a lender is likely to want to see. They will also look at how much of your sales already goes on payroll, which shapes how much headroom you have.
Is it worth borrowing to extend opening hours?

Only if the extra sales are likely to exceed the added wages and running costs. Try a short trial first, and borrow for the trial only. A broker can suggest a flexible structure. Compare the wage cost against a realistic sales forecast, and test it against a quieter outcome.
Will lenders ask for staffing plans?

They may ask what the money is for, so a clear explanation of the hires and the sales they support helps. Bank statements and accounts are normally needed too. Lenders will also check recent accounts and bank statements, and a broker can explain which documents suit your case.
Do I need a personal guarantee?

Unsecured lenders often ask directors for one. It could make you personally liable if the company cannot repay. Read the terms carefully and consider legal advice before signing. The risk is greater on larger sums, so check the amount before agreeing.

buying-stock|manufacturing.h1: Finance for buying stock in manufacturing
buying-stock|manufacturing.title: Raw Materials and Stock Finance for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
buying-stock|manufacturing.desc: How manufacturers finance raw materials, components and work in progress when suppliers want paying before customers do, and which finance suits. Get matched.
buying-stock|manufacturing.lead: A manufacturer pays for raw materials, spends weeks making the goods and then waits for its customer’s payment terms.
intro: Manufacturing ties up money at three stages. Raw materials and components are bought, often in minimum order quantities with long lead times. They then become work in progress while labour and energy are added, and finally finished goods wait for delivery and an invoice. A customer on 60-day terms means the cash may not return for several months after the first purchase. Lenders will want to see which stage causes the squeeze.

Because the business is usually invoicing other companies, invoice finance and revolving credit facilities are common choices, with secured loans for larger or longer-term inventory needs. Imported components add exchange-rate movements and deposits to suppliers abroad. Lenders will want to see order books and customer quality, as well as accounts. The order book matters as much as the balance sheet. Lenders often ask for sight of customer contracts and payment histories, which a broker can help you assemble.
uses: Raw materials for a large order
Buy steel, resin, timber or components for a significant customer order that will not be paid until after delivery.
Minimum order quantities
Take a larger supplier order than immediate demand requires to get the unit price, or because the supplier will not split it.
Imported components with long lead times
Pay deposits months ahead for components sourced abroad, so production does not stall waiting for deliveries.
Smoothing a seasonal run
Build finished stock before a customer’s peak period, so production is steady instead of a rush.
fit: Invoice finance against delivered orders

Once goods are delivered and invoiced, invoice finance releases part of the invoice value early, which helps repay the cost of materials. For example, a fabricator might fund £120,000 of steel and release cash as each delivery is invoiced. Lenders check customer credit quality and concentration.
A revolving facility through the cycle
Manufacturers that buy continuously can use a revolving credit facility, drawing for each purchase and repaying on receipt of payments. Lenders look at stock turn, order book and payment history.
Secured loans for larger needs

A secured business loan, backed by property or other assets, can offer larger sums over longer terms. This tends to suit sizeable, repeated inventory needs. The security could be at risk if repayments are missed.
considerations: Customer concentration
If one customer accounts for most of your sales, lenders may be cautious. A delay or dispute with that customer affects repayments directly.
Work in progress is hard to borrow against
Part-finished goods are difficult to value and rarely count for much as security. Be prepared for lenders to look mainly at invoices and trading history.
Currency and price swings
Buying in another currency adds exchange-rate risk, and commodity prices can move before you sell. Build a margin of safety into pricing and borrowing.
faqs: Can I finance raw materials before I have an order?

It is harder. Lenders generally prefer purchases tied to confirmed orders or a track record of regular sales. A revolving facility based on trading history may help. A broker can explain what lenders usually look for. Evidence of orders, such as purchase orders or contracts, usually carries most weight.
How does invoice finance help with materials?

It releases cash against invoices you have already raised, so the money from one order can fund the materials for the next. It does not pay for materials before an invoice exists, so some firms combine it with a facility. Lenders will want to see the steady relationship, the quality of the customer and the cost of the order.
What if my supplier is overseas?

Some specialist providers offer trade finance, paying the supplier directly and being repaid by you later. Availability depends on the goods and your history. A broker can tell you whether it is likely to be available. Expect a lender to ask for a valuation and an assessment of how easily the stock could be sold.
Is stock accepted as security?

Sometimes, particularly for finished goods that are easy to value and resell. Raw materials and work in progress count for less. A secured loan may use property or equipment as well. Check any seasonal or one-off elements first, because these can lengthen the cycle.
How long should a loan for stock last?

Usually no longer than the cycle from buying materials to being paid, which can be several months in manufacturing. A broker can help you match the term to your production and payment timeline. Terms vary, so discuss the pattern of your own purchases with a broker.

hiring-staff|manufacturing.h1: Finance for hiring staff in manufacturing
hiring-staff|manufacturing.title: Hiring Finance for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|manufacturing.desc: How manufacturers finance machine operators, skilled engineers, extra shifts and training while new capacity ramps up, and which finance suits. Get matched.
hiring-staff|manufacturing.lead: A new shift or skilled operator costs money from the first day, while output and payment follow weeks later.
intro: Factories hire in blocks. A new machine may need three operators across two shifts, a larger contract may need a second shift entirely, and a specialist such as a CNC programmer or quality engineer can be hard to find and expensive to keep. New people also take time to learn the process, so output starts below full pace. Customers then pay on 30 to 60 day terms, which stretches the gap further.

That makes the choice of finance a question of timing. Invoice finance can release cash as the extra output is invoiced, an unsecured loan covers planned hires and a secured loan may suit a bigger expansion. Machinery bought alongside new staff may be handled separately through asset finance. Lenders usually ask how firm the extra orders are, and a broker can help you present that evidence clearly alongside your accounts.
uses: Adding a second shift
Take on operators and a supervisor to run the factory for more hours, carrying wages until the extra output is invoiced.
Staffing a new machine
Hire and train operators for newly installed equipment while production is still ramping up.
Engineers and technical hires
Recruit a specialist whose salary and recruitment fee are a stretch for the business, in order to take on more complex work.
Apprentices and upskilling
Support apprenticeship programmes, including supervision and training time, to build a skilled workforce over a few years.
fit: Invoice finance as output grows

If the extra capacity serves business customers on credit terms, invoice finance can release cash against the invoices it generates. For example, a plastics moulder adding a night shift might draw against £90,000 of invoices. Lenders check customer quality and the stability of the order book.
Unsecured loans for defined hires

A fixed sum over a set term suits hires planned to a start date. Lenders review accounts, margins and the order book, and often ask directors for a personal guarantee. Terms should allow the team time to reach full productivity.
Secured loans for larger expansion

Where hiring is part of a bigger expansion, a secured loan against property or other business assets can provide larger sums over longer terms. The security is at risk if repayments are missed, so consider that carefully.
considerations: Output ramps slowly
New operators rarely reach full productivity at once. Plan for several months of lower output and set the term to match.
Skills shortages
Specialist roles can take months to fill and may need above-market pay. Check that the salary still makes sense for the work the person will bring in.
Order book risk
A second shift is expensive if orders fall away. Look at contracts, customer commitments and the likelihood of repeat work before borrowing.
faqs: Can I borrow to run a second shift?

Many manufacturers do, using invoice finance or a loan to carry wages while extra output is invoiced and paid. Lenders will look closely at your order book. A broker can explain what a lender is likely to need. Lenders will also check how stable the underlying demand is.
Should I finance machinery and staff together?

They are often arranged separately. Asset finance usually covers the machine, secured by the machine itself, while a loan or facility covers wages and training. A broker can structure the two to suit your cash flow. It is common for the two to be structured so that repayments suit each asset’s life.
How long does it take for hires to pay back?

It varies with the role. A trained operator may be productive in weeks, while a specialist may take months. Choose a term that reflects the realistic time to full output. Sector, skills and location all affect how long a hire takes to reach full output.
Will lenders want to see my contracts?

Often, yes. Signed contracts, customer agreements and repeat orders show the work behind a hire. Recent accounts and bank statements are also normally required. Customer commitments, forecasts and any framework agreements all help a lender follow the plan. Recent accounts and bank statements are also normally required.
Is agency labour a cheaper alternative?

It avoids long-term commitments but costs more per hour. Compare total costs over the expected period with your accountant, and consider the effect on training and quality. Whichever route you choose, work out the full cost, including training, supervision and the time before output is steady.

buying-stock|transport-and-logistics.h1: Finance for buying stock in transport and logistics
buying-stock|transport-and-logistics.title: Fuel, Spares and Stock Finance for Haulage | Loanleaf
buying-stock|transport-and-logistics.desc: How hauliers and logistics firms finance fuel, tyres, spares, pallets and packaging, the consumable stock a fleet runs on, and which finance suits. Get matched.
buying-stock|transport-and-logistics.lead: A fleet does not hold stock to sell, but it does need fuel, tyres, parts and packaging paid for well before customers settle.
intro: For a transport business, stock means the consumables that keep vehicles and warehouses moving: diesel, AdBlue, tyres, brake parts, pallets, wrap and, for some, goods held on behalf of clients. Fuel alone can be one of the largest regular outgoings, and suppliers often want settlement weekly, while customers pay on 30 to 60 day terms. A spike in fuel prices makes the gap wider. Lenders look closely at who pays you and how quickly.

Where the cash is tied up in unpaid invoices, invoice finance is a natural fit, alongside revolving credit facilities for variable purchases and unsecured loans for bulk buying. Vehicles themselves are usually financed separately through asset finance, so this page concerns the day-to-day supplies around them. Vehicles are normally financed separately, and some firms combine several products. A broker can explain how they fit alongside each other, and how each would sit with your existing commitments.
uses: Fuel on weekly terms
Cover a fuel card or bulk diesel bill that is paid every week, while customers’ invoices run to 60 days.
Tyres and spares in bulk
Buy a set of tyres or a stock of common spares at a better price, to reduce vehicle downtime.
Pallets and packaging
Hold enough pallets, wrap and cartons to handle a warehousing or fulfilment contract that has just started.
Stock held for clients
Fund the cost of goods bought on behalf of a customer for storage and delivery, where the customer repays on later terms.
fit: Invoice finance for the payment gap

Because the gap is caused by customers paying late, invoice finance releases cash from invoices as soon as they are raised. For example, a haulier with £150,000 of unpaid invoices might release part of that to meet fuel bills. Lenders check customer credit quality and the invoice records.
A revolving facility for variable buying
Fuel and parts spending changes week to week, so a revolving credit facility lets the business draw and repay as it needs. Lenders look at monthly turnover and how consistently it covers drawings.
An unsecured loan for a bulk purchase

An unsecured loan suits a single bulk buy, such as a year’s tyre supply at a negotiated price. Lenders will check accounts, bank statements and any existing vehicle finance, and may ask for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Fuel price swings
If diesel prices jump, borrowing needs rise too. Build in headroom, and avoid sizing a facility to today’s price alone.
Consumables are not security
Fuel and spares cannot be repossessed in a useful way, so lenders rely on invoices and trading history instead. Expect them to focus on customer payment performance.
Check supplier terms first
A fuel supplier or tyre depot may offer 14 or 30 day terms. Using these may cost less than borrowing, so compare before arranging finance.
faqs: Can I finance fuel for my haulage business?

Some lenders will cover fuel costs through general working capital, invoice finance or a revolving facility. Fuel cards with credit terms are another route. A broker can discuss which fits your invoices and customers. It is also worth asking about fuel card terms.
Is this different from vehicle finance?

Yes. Asset finance buys or leases the vehicles themselves, secured against them. Finance for fuel, parts and packaging is working capital, usually based on invoices or turnover. Many fleets use both. Many fleets use several products together. Many fleets use both, with a different lender for each need.
How does invoice finance help with fuel?

It converts unpaid customer invoices into cash sooner, so weekly fuel bills do not wait on 60-day payments. It depends on the customers’ credit quality and your invoicing records. A broker can explain how it would work for you. Aged debtor reports and customer lists are the first things lenders usually ask to see.
Will lenders ask about my main customers?

Yes, especially for invoice finance. They want to know who pays, how long they take and whether any customer represents most of your revenue. Have recent aged debtor reports ready. Customer concentration matters, because one late payer can affect the whole facility.
What if fuel prices fall after I borrow?

Your repayments are fixed or set by the agreement, so they would not fall with the price. A flexible facility, where you borrow only what you use, can be less exposed to that kind of movement. A broker can explain how a facility’s limit and repayments would respond if costs fell.

hiring-staff|transport-and-logistics.h1: Finance for hiring staff in transport and logistics
hiring-staff|transport-and-logistics.title: Driver and Staff Hiring Finance for Haulage | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|transport-and-logistics.desc: How hauliers and logistics firms finance driver recruitment, CPC training and warehouse teams while customers pay late, and which finance suits. Get matched.
hiring-staff|transport-and-logistics.lead: Drivers are paid weekly and trained before they earn, while customers often take 30 to 60 days to settle.
intro: A haulage or logistics business can win a contract it cannot yet staff. HGV drivers are in short supply, and hiring one means paying for the licence checks, Driver CPC training, a tachograph card and sometimes an agency fee before the first load is delivered. Warehouse teams, transport planners and a compliance manager add further payroll. Wages are paid weekly or monthly, while invoices to customers stay open for weeks.

Invoice finance is common in the sector because it releases cash from invoices that are already raised. Unsecured loans suit planned recruitment, and revolving facilities help smooth uneven weeks. Lenders will consider the contract behind the hire, how reliable the customers are and how many vehicles are already idle for lack of drivers. Idle vehicles waiting for drivers are a sign the hire is worthwhile, and lenders will notice that, along with your existing fleet commitments.
uses: Drivers for a new contract
Recruit and onboard drivers for a contract you have won, carrying wages until the first invoices are paid.
Training and licence costs
Cover Driver CPC modules, licence acquisition for existing staff and tachograph training for new starters.
Warehouse and fulfilment teams
Staff a new warehouse operation, including pickers, forklift operators and a shift supervisor.
Planners and compliance
Add a transport manager or planner whose role supports more vehicles on the road, ahead of the revenue they enable.
fit: Invoice finance matches payroll to payment

Releasing cash against raised invoices lets weekly wages be met without waiting for 60-day terms. For example, a firm adding three drivers might draw part of £100,000 of outstanding invoices. Lenders check customer credit quality and invoice history.
An unsecured loan for planned recruitment
A fixed sum over a set term covers agency fees, training and the first few months of wages. Lenders will ask what contract the hire supports. Directors may be asked for a personal guarantee.
A revolving facility for uneven weeks
Weeks with idle vehicles or delayed payments make cash flow uneven. A revolving credit facility lets you draw during the gaps and repay as payments land, within an agreed limit.
considerations: Idle vehicles cost money
A driver without a load is still paid. Make sure the work is confirmed before hiring, and check that the contract term is long enough to justify it.
Driver turnover
Drivers can move quickly to a better offer, taking training investment with them. Consider retention as well as recruitment when you size the borrowing.
Late-paying customers
If one large customer pays late, wages still need meeting. Keep a buffer, and ask a broker how the facility would behave if payments slipped.
faqs: Can I get finance to recruit HGV drivers?

Yes, businesses often use an unsecured loan, invoice finance or a revolving facility to cover recruitment, training and early wages. Lenders will want to see the contract or demand behind the hire. A broker can explain what they typically ask for.
Does invoice finance suit logistics firms?

It often does, because customers commonly pay on 30 to 60 day terms. Lenders check customer quality and invoicing records. A broker can say whether your invoices are likely to be accepted. Recent aged debtor lists help a broker judge what might be available.
Can I finance Driver CPC training?

Some businesses include training costs in a general working-capital loan. It is usually a modest amount compared with wages, so you may prefer to pay it from cash flow. A broker can discuss the options. A broker can also say whether any of your training can be funded by other schemes.
How much should I borrow for a new driver?

Many firms estimate the wages, employer costs, training and agency fee until the driver is covering their own cost. Your accountant can help set a sensible figure, and a lender will want to see how it was worked out. A broker can help you decide what to include.
Is agency cover a cheaper short-term option?

Agency drivers avoid long commitments but cost more per day and may know your routes less well. Compare total costs for the likely period, and consider the customer service effect. Cover for sickness, holidays and notice periods is worth costing in as well.

buying-stock|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Finance for buying stock in healthcare and dental
buying-stock|healthcare-and-dental.title: Stock and Supplies Finance for Dental and Healthcare | Loanleaf
buying-stock|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How dental practices, clinics and pharmacies finance consumables, materials and clinical supplies, and which finance types suit. Get matched with a broker.
buying-stock|healthcare-and-dental.lead: Clinical supplies are bought steadily and used steadily, but some orders are large, dated and paid for well before treatment is billed.
intro: A practice or clinic rarely sells stock in the way a shop does. Instead it uses consumables: dental composites, implants, impression materials, gloves, dressings, injectables and lab work. Usage is steady and predictable, which is helpful, but expiry dates, regulatory storage rules and supplier minimums can make large orders awkward. Implant and aligner cases can also carry big upfront material costs well before the patient has paid the final balance.

Pharmacies hold true saleable stock, with wholesaler terms and reimbursement delays from NHS contracts. For all of these businesses, revenue tends to be steady, and lenders favour that. A revolving credit facility, a short unsecured loan or, for larger needs, a secured loan are the most common starting points. Lenders see that regular pattern as a strength, and a broker can help you present it. They will also want to know whether you own or lease the premises, and what other borrowing is already in place.
uses: Bulk consumables order
Buy a year’s supply of composites, anaesthetic or PPE at a volume price, where usage is reliable and expiry dates allow.
Implant and aligner cases
Pay for implants, aligner sets or lab-made restorations upfront for patients who will pay over the course of treatment.
Pharmacy wholesaler orders
Cover wholesaler invoices while NHS reimbursements and private sales come in, particularly in peak winter months.
Stocking a new clinic
Fill a new surgery or treatment room with consumables and clinical supplies before its first patients arrive.
fit: A revolving facility for steady use

A revolving credit facility lets a practice draw to cover supplier invoices and repay as treatment is billed. For example, a three-surgery practice might hold a £40,000 limit and draw £15,000 for a bulk supplies order. Lenders look at patient revenue, consistency and any existing borrowing.
Short unsecured loans for one-off orders

An unsecured loan suits a single planned purchase, such as stocking up before a price rise. Lenders review accounts, bank statements and the practice’s trading record, and directors may be asked for a personal guarantee.
Secured loans for larger needs

Where a practice owns its premises or other assets, a secured loan can offer larger sums over longer terms. Because the security could be at risk, it suits more significant, longer-term needs rather than routine buying.
considerations: Expiry and storage
Many clinical products have shelf lives and must be stored correctly. Buying more than you can use before expiry turns a saving into waste.
NHS payment timing
Practices with NHS contracts are usually paid on a regular schedule, but clawbacks and adjustments can affect cash flow. Factor this into how you plan repayments.
Price versus cash flow
A bulk discount is only worthwhile if it exceeds the cost of borrowing and the stock is certain to be used. Work it out with your accountant first.
faqs: Can I borrow to buy dental supplies?

Yes, many practices use a revolving facility or a short unsecured loan for supplies. Lenders look at your revenue, accounts and how long you have traded. A broker can compare options for your practice, though no outcome is guaranteed. Many practices also spread orders across the year.
Does a pharmacy count as stock finance?

Yes. Pharmacies hold saleable stock and pay wholesalers on terms, so lenders see a clear stock cycle. NHS reimbursement timing is a factor lenders will ask about. A broker can discuss how your income pattern would be viewed. A broker can discuss how your income pattern would be viewed.
Is invoice finance relevant for a clinic?

Usually less so, because most patient income is paid at the time of treatment. It can apply where a business invoices other organisations, such as employers or NHS commissioners. A broker can say whether it fits. Lenders look at how stable your private and NHS income are and whether any contract is nearing renewal.
Can I finance lab fees and implants?

Often as part of working-capital finance. Some practices use a short loan or facility to carry case costs until patients pay their balance. Lenders will want to see how the case income arrives. Lab fees and implant costs can be significant, so state the figures clearly.
What if I have a seasonal dip?

Some practices see quieter periods around holidays. A flexible facility, drawn only when needed, can be less exposed to those dips than a fixed loan. Share your monthly revenue pattern with the broker. Provide twelve months of figures so any seasonal pattern is clear.

hiring-staff|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Finance for hiring staff in healthcare and dental
hiring-staff|healthcare-and-dental.title: Hiring Finance for Dental and Healthcare Practices | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How dental practices, clinics and care providers finance clinicians, nurses, hygienists and reception teams while new hires build their patient lists.
hiring-staff|healthcare-and-dental.lead: A new clinician is paid from the first day, but a full diary of patients can take months to build.
intro: Healthcare hiring has long lead times. A new associate dentist or hygienist needs registration checks, indemnity cover, induction and a surgery fitted out for their use, and then time to build a patient list. During that period they may be earning less than they cost. Nurses, receptionists and practice managers add steady payroll, and locum cover can be costly while a permanent role is vacant. Lenders will want to hear how the role supports revenue.

Patient revenue is usually reliable once a clinic is established, and lenders tend to view that favourably. Unsecured loans suit planned hires, while secured loans can support a bigger expansion such as an additional surgery. Revolving facilities can smooth payroll when income arrives unevenly, for example when NHS contract payments and private fees land on different dates. Care homes and clinics face the same pattern with a different mix of staff, and a broker can explain how lenders view each.
uses: An associate or specialist
Bring in a dentist, GP or consultant with a view to growing the patient list, and fund their salary while the diary fills.
Hygienists and therapists
Add a hygienist or therapist so that more patients can be seen per day, using a surgery that is currently under-used.
Nurses and care staff
Recruit clinical staff for a new ward, home or clinic, with induction and registration checks before they start.
Locum cover and agency fees
Cover the cost of locums or recruitment agencies while looking for a permanent hire.
fit: An unsecured loan for planned hires

A fixed sum and a set term suit a hire with a known start date. Terms should reflect how long the new clinician takes to reach a full diary. Lenders look at revenue, margins and wage costs, and directors may be asked for a personal guarantee.
A revolving facility for payroll timing

Where income comes from several sources, such as NHS contract payments, private fees and insurers, timing can be uneven. A facility lets you draw to meet payroll and repay on receipt, within an agreed limit.
A secured loan for larger expansion

If hiring is part of an expansion, such as a new surgery fitted out for a new dentist, a secured loan may offer larger sums over longer terms. For example, a practice might borrow £150,000 for fit-out and early wages. The security is at risk if repayments are missed.
considerations: Patient list growth is gradual
A clinician may take six months or more to reach a full diary. Set the term and your buffer on realistic timelines, not best-case ones.
Regulatory and indemnity costs
Registration, inspections and indemnity cover add to the cost of each clinical hire. Include them in the budget alongside salary.
Retention and associates leaving
If an associate leaves, some of their patients may go with them. Consider contract terms and the effect on revenue before relying on a single hire.
faqs: Can I get a loan to hire an associate dentist?

Yes, practices often use unsecured loans or facilities for this. Lenders will look at your revenue, accounts and how the new hire supports growth. A broker can explain what a lender may ask for, without any guarantee of outcome. Practices often also check their own contracts.
Will lenders count NHS income?

Yes, lenders generally view NHS contract income as predictable, though they will check its terms and any clawback risk. Private income is also considered. A broker can advise how your mix of income is likely to be viewed. It is worth confirming contract terms and any clawback rules first.
How long until a new clinician pays for themselves?

It varies by role and location. A dentist may take several months to build a full list. Plan for the longer end of that, and set a term that does not rely on fast growth. Build a conservative estimate, and remember to include the first weeks of induction and registration.
Can I finance locum fees?

Some businesses include them in general working-capital borrowing. Locum rates can be high, so consider whether a permanent hire would be cheaper over time. A broker can discuss options. A permanent hire may be better value over a year, but check the numbers.
Do I need security for a hiring loan?

Not always. Many hiring loans are unsecured, though directors may be asked for a personal guarantee. Larger amounts may need security, such as the practice premises. Your accountant can help you decide what can be offered, and a solicitor should review any guarantee.

buying-stock|ecommerce.h1: Finance for buying stock in ecommerce
buying-stock|ecommerce.title: Inventory Finance for Online Sellers | Loanleaf
buying-stock|ecommerce.desc: How online retailers and marketplace sellers finance inventory, long supplier lead times and peak-season buying, and which finance types suit. Get matched.
buying-stock|ecommerce.lead: Online sellers often pay suppliers months before stock arrives, then wait again for marketplace payouts.
intro: Ecommerce stock cycles are long and front-loaded. A brand sourcing from overseas may pay a deposit at order, the balance before shipment, and then wait weeks for sea freight, customs and delivery to a warehouse or fulfilment centre. Marketplace sellers may need to send inventory into a fulfilment network ahead of peak, then wait for payouts that arrive on a cycle. Advertising spend to sell the stock adds a further outlay.

Lenders can see online sales through payment providers, marketplaces and bank statements, so a revolving credit facility, an unsecured loan or a revenue-based advance repaid from sales are common routes. Import VAT and duty can also create a large short-term bill, for which VAT and tax loans are sometimes considered. That is long enough for a good seller to run short of cash. Weeks of cash tied up before launch are common.
uses: Peak-season inventory
Place a large order in the summer for Black Friday and Christmas, paying suppliers before any of the sales come in.
Overseas supplier deposits
Pay deposits and balances to manufacturers abroad, covering the months before stock reaches the warehouse.
Marketplace fulfilment stock
Send a large inbound shipment to a fulfilment network ahead of a promotion, and carry the cost until payouts arrive.
Import VAT and duty
Cover the import VAT and duty due when goods clear customs, before the stock is sold.
fit: A revolving facility for repeat buying

Brands that reorder regularly can use a revolving credit facility, drawing for each order and repaying as sales come in. For example, a skincare brand might hold a £75,000 limit. Lenders look at monthly sales, margins and return rates.
Revenue-linked repayment
A merchant cash advance or revenue-based product is repaid as a share of sales, so repayments follow demand. It is usually costlier than a conventional loan, so compare the total repayable.
An unsecured loan for a defined order

For a single planned order, such as the next season’s range, an unsecured loan offers a fixed sum and a set term. Lenders review accounts and bank statements, and directors may be asked for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Long lead times tie up cash
Between paying a supplier and receiving payouts, money can be committed for months. Plan the borrowing term for the whole cycle, not just the sales period.
Return rates and dead stock
High returns reduce real revenue, and slow lines tie up cash. Be cautious about borrowing to buy more of a product that is not yet proven.
Platform dependence
Marketplace rules, fee changes or account suspensions can disrupt sales. Lenders know this, and a diversified customer base can help.
faqs: Can I borrow to buy stock for my online shop?

Yes, if the company has traded for at least six months and has the revenue lenders look for. Revolving facilities, unsecured loans and revenue-based advances are common. A broker can compare these once they have your figures. Many sellers also ask lenders about options for further orders.
Do lenders accept marketplace sales as evidence?

Many do. They can look at payment provider and marketplace reports as well as bank statements. A broker can tell you which providers are comfortable with your sales channels. Your sales reports and payout histories help a broker understand your business.
Can I finance goods bought from overseas?

Sometimes, through general working capital or specialist trade finance that pays the supplier directly. Availability depends on the goods and your trading history. A broker can say what may be possible. Some providers will also look at your supplier history.
What if my stock does not sell?

You would still need to meet repayments, so a cautious order size helps. Consider testing a new line with a smaller batch, and keep a cash buffer. Test new lines on a small run first, and avoid ordering more until sell-through is clear.
Can finance cover import VAT?

Some businesses use a VAT or tax loan, or a working-capital facility, to cover import VAT before goods are sold. It is worth checking whether postponed VAT accounting is available to you, via your accountant. A broker can discuss how the timing would work for you.

hiring-staff|ecommerce.h1: Finance for hiring staff in ecommerce
hiring-staff|ecommerce.title: Hiring Finance for Ecommerce Businesses | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|ecommerce.desc: How online sellers and ecommerce brands finance customer service teams, warehouse staff, developers and peak-season hires, and which finance suits. Get matched.
hiring-staff|ecommerce.lead: Online businesses often need to hire ahead of a peak, then see the sales arrive in a few intense weeks.
intro: Ecommerce hiring tends to be lumpy. A warehouse might need a dozen temporary pickers and packers from October, a customer service team needs extra cover for returns in January, and a growing brand might finally hire its first developer or marketing manager. Unlike a shop, there is no counter to serve, so a hire may be about capacity behind the scenes, with revenue effects that are harder to trace. Lenders will want to see the sales pattern.

Lenders can see online revenue through payment providers and marketplaces, so they can judge how seasonal a business is. Revolving credit facilities help cover payroll through the peak, unsecured loans suit planned permanent hires and revenue-linked advances can follow the sales pattern. The right mix depends on how concentrated your sales are in a few months. Revenue is easy to trace online, which helps. A broker can help you match the terms to your sales pattern.
uses: Peak-season warehouse team
Recruit temporary pickers, packers and supervisors for October to December, covering wages ahead of the busiest sales weeks.
Customer service and returns
Add support staff before the peak and into the January returns period, when revenue has slowed but work has not.
A first developer or marketing hire
Bring in a permanent developer, performance marketer or merchandiser, with a salary the business has not yet grown into.
Moving fulfilment in-house
Hire a team to run storage and dispatch yourself, instead of using a third-party fulfilment provider.
fit: A revolving facility through the peak

Payroll rises before sales do, so a revolving credit facility lets you draw in October and repay in December and January. For example, a brand might draw £30,000 for extra staff and clear it by February. Lenders look at monthly sales across the previous year.
Revenue-linked repayment

A merchant cash advance or revenue-based product is repaid as a share of sales, so payments follow the seasonal pattern. It is usually costlier than a conventional loan, so compare the total repayable.
An unsecured loan for permanent roles

For roles that run all year, an unsecured loan offers a fixed sum and predictable repayments. Lenders look at margins, accounts and how the hire supports growth, and directors may be asked for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Peak concentration
If most sales fall in a few weeks, wages for the rest of the year may be hard to carry. Check how permanent hires would be paid for in March.
Hire versus outsource
A third-party fulfilment or support provider may cost more per order but avoids fixed wages. Compare total costs at your volume before borrowing to hire.
Contractors and employment status
Freelance developers and marketers can look cheaper, but employment rules apply. Speak to your accountant before deciding how to engage people.
faqs: Can I borrow to hire peak-season staff?

Yes, short-term facilities or revenue-linked advances are often used. Lenders will look at last year’s sales and your plans. A broker can explain what is likely to be asked, without any guarantee of outcome. Last year’s monthly sales will be the starting point.
Is a revenue-based advance good for seasonal hiring?

It can be, because repayment follows sales. It is usually more expensive than a conventional loan, so compare the total repayable and think about whether a short facility would cost less. Seasonal brands can also ask for a repayment pattern that follows sales.
How should I size borrowing for new hires?

Estimate wages, employer National Insurance, pension, equipment and training for the months before the role pays for itself. Your accountant can help, and lenders will want to see how you reached the figure. Keep a contingency in case the peak is shorter or lower than forecast.
Will lenders check my marketplace sales?

Often, yes. They may ask for marketplace and payment provider reports as well as bank statements. A broker can say which providers work with your channels. Marketplace payout reports and card processor statements can help a lender follow your sales.
Do I need a personal guarantee?

Unsecured lenders frequently ask directors for one. It could make you personally liable if the company cannot repay. Read the terms carefully, and consider legal advice before signing. Read the terms carefully, and be clear about how the guarantee would work if sales were weaker.

buying-stock|professional-services.h1: Finance for buying stock in professional services
buying-stock|professional-services.title: Stock and Supplies Finance for Professional Firms | Loanleaf
buying-stock|professional-services.desc: Most professional services firms hold little stock. Here is where purchases do arise, and which finance types suit, from licences to kit. Get matched.
buying-stock|professional-services.lead: Few professional firms carry stock, so the real question is usually what the money is for and which finance fits that purpose.
intro: Accountants, solicitors, consultants and agencies mostly sell time rather than goods. Yet purchases do arise: a firm may buy a bundle of software licences to resell to clients, kit for a field team, printed materials for a campaign or goods bought on a client’s behalf and recharged afterwards. Architects, surveyors and engineers may buy materials or equipment for a project and bill the client later. Lenders will want to know what the cost relates to.

In most of these cases the business is waiting to be paid, not waiting for stock to sell. That points towards invoice finance, a revolving facility or a short unsecured loan, rather than anything built around inventory. If the real issue is a gap between work done and money received, a broker may suggest a working-capital route instead, and that is worth saying early in any conversation. Each case is different, so be specific about what was bought and who pays.
uses: Licences bought for resale
Buy a volume of software seats or subscriptions to resell to clients at a margin, paying the vendor before clients pay you.
Disbursements on client work
Pay for third-party costs such as searches, print or materials on behalf of clients, then recharge them on the next invoice.
Equipment for a project
Buy specialist kit or materials for a large engagement, where the client pays on milestones after delivery.
A product line alongside services
Stock the goods for a side business, such as a training product or a branded range, that sits next to the main practice.
fit: Invoice finance for recharges

Where purchases are recharged on invoices to business clients, invoice finance can release cash from those invoices sooner. For example, a marketing agency fronting £40,000 of media costs might release part of the invoice. Lenders check the clients’ credit quality and the contracts.
A revolving facility for variable buying

Firms with varying client disbursements can use a revolving credit facility, drawing for each purchase and repaying on payment. Lenders look at monthly fees, client concentration and how steadily drawings have been cleared.
A short unsecured loan for a single purchase
For a one-off purchase such as a licence bundle, an unsecured loan offers a fixed sum and term. Lenders review accounts and bank statements, and may ask directors for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Check whether it is really stock
If the need is a gap between billing and payment, the finance should be built around that gap. A broker may point you to invoice finance or a facility rather than a stock product.
Client credit risk
If you front costs for a client who then pays late or disputes the bill, the cost lands on you. Where possible, ask for money on account before buying.
Margins on resale are thin
Reselling licences or goods often carries a small margin. Make sure it comfortably exceeds the cost of borrowing, or the transaction loses money.
faqs: Do professional services firms use stock finance?

Rarely in the traditional sense. Most use working-capital finance, invoice finance or facilities to cover purchases made for clients. A broker can help work out which fits your situation. Most firms already know whether the need is for a short loan or a longer facility, and a broker can help confirm which.
Can I finance software licences I resell?

Sometimes, through a short loan or facility. Lenders will look at your resale margin, client contracts and trading record. Where a client pays quickly, the exposure is shorter. Licence agreements, client contracts and margins help a lender follow the transaction.
Is it better to ask clients to pay on account?

Often, yes. Money on account removes the need to borrow and reduces risk if a client pays late. Where that is not possible, invoice finance or a facility can cover the gap. A broker can also explain the costs involved for each route.
What if my purchases are for a one-off project?

A short unsecured loan or facility can cover it, with repayment tied to project milestones. Lenders will want to see the contract and milestone payment schedule. Ask your client for a deposit or staged payments if you can, to keep the amount borrowed down.
Will lenders view my firm differently without stock?

Not negatively. Lenders look at profit, cash flow and client quality. A firm without stock simply has less to offer as security, so unsecured or invoice-based finance is more common. Accounts and bank statements show the strength of your fee income and cash flow instead.

hiring-staff|professional-services.h1: Finance for hiring staff in professional services
hiring-staff|professional-services.title: Hiring Finance for Professional Services Firms | Loanleaf
hiring-staff|professional-services.desc: How accountants, law firms, consultancies and agencies finance new fee-earners while billing catches up, and which finance types tend to suit. Get matched.
hiring-staff|professional-services.lead: In a professional firm the people are the product, and a new fee-earner costs money months before their work is billed and paid.
intro: For an accountancy, law firm, consultancy or agency, hiring is the main route to growth and also the main cost. A new fee-earner needs a recruitment fee, often 15 to 25 per cent of salary, plus equipment, supervision and professional registration. Their utilisation builds gradually, then work in progress must be billed, and clients may take 30 to 60 days to pay. The gap between salary and cash received can run to several months.

Unsecured loans suit planned hires with a clear start date, invoice finance can release cash from billed work and revolving facilities help with payroll timing around VAT quarters and tax payments. Lenders look at recurring clients, fee income and utilisation, as well as accounts and bank statements. Recurring fees from retainers or long-standing clients carry particular weight, and a broker can help you present that clearly. Recruitment fees and supervision time also weigh on early margins.
uses: A fee-earner for a new client
Recruit a manager, solicitor or consultant to deliver work for a client you have won, covering salary before billing.
Building a junior team
Take on trainees or graduates, covering supervision time and training before they can bill at full rate.
Opening a new service line
Hire a specialist to launch a new service, such as tax advisory or employment law, ahead of the first clients.
Recruitment fees
Spread the cost of agency fees for senior hires, so a large one-off bill does not hit a single month’s cash flow.
fit: An unsecured loan for a planned hire

A fixed sum over a set term suits hires with a known start date. For example, a firm might borrow £45,000 to cover a recruitment fee and six months of salary. Lenders review fee income, recurring clients and accounts, and directors may be asked for a personal guarantee.
Invoice finance as billing grows

Once the new hire’s work is billed, invoice finance can release part of those invoices sooner. Lenders check client credit quality and any concentration. It does not help before invoices exist, so it works best alongside a loan.
A revolving facility around tax dates

VAT quarters, corporation tax and partner or director drawings can cause uneven cash balances. A facility can smooth payroll through those dates. A VAT or tax loan may also help where a large bill falls due during the ramp-up.
considerations: Utilisation takes time
A new fee-earner may not reach target billing for several months. Set the term and your buffer with that in mind, not on the ideal case.
Dependence on one client
If the hire depends on one client’s work, losing that client leaves the cost in place. Check how diversified your pipeline is first.
Fixed cost against variable income
Salaries are fixed while fees can fluctuate. Stress-test the plan against a slower year before taking on repayments.
faqs: Can I borrow to hire a fee-earner?

Yes, professional firms often use an unsecured loan or facility for this. Lenders will look at recurring fees, accounts and how the hire supports growth. A broker can explain what they typically ask for, with no guarantee of outcome. Keep a clear schedule of how the role will build billing.
Does invoice finance suit a consultancy?

It can, where clients are businesses paying on credit terms. It releases cash from billed work, so it helps after the hire starts delivering. A broker can say whether your invoices are likely to be accepted. Lenders will also ask about the hire’s likely start date and billing targets.
How long before a new hire pays back?

It varies by role and sector. Many firms plan for three to six months before a fee-earner is covering their own cost. Choose a term that accounts for billing and payment delays as well. Think about how quickly the role could bill, and how long clients take to pay.
Can I finance the recruitment fee?

Some businesses include it in a working-capital loan, since it can be a large one-off. Ask the agency about staged payments first. A broker can discuss which route may suit. Agencies often agree staged payments, particularly for senior roles. A broker can discuss options for your own case.
Will lenders ask about my client base?

Yes. They want to see recurring work, a spread of clients and good payment records. Recent accounts, bank statements and a clear plan for the hire all help. A broker can help you gather the figures a lender is likely to ask for.
